# Use case 4: cell-cell graphs for clustering single-cell data

Graph-based clustering is the standard approach to identify cell
populations in single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) data. In this approach,
a graph of cells is built from a low-dimensional representation of
the data (e.g., top principal components), with each cell connected to its
nearest neighbors, and then communities are detected in the graph
[@amezquita2020orchestrating]. Although cell-cell graphs are central to
scRNA-seq data analysis, they are typically discarded after clustering,
and there is no dedicated container for them in the
`SingleCellExperiment` class. Here, we will use __GraphExperiment__ to store
cell-cell graphs in the `colGraphs` slot along with the expression data and
dimensionality reduction results. We will use the mouse brain
data set from @zeisel2015cell, which includes ~3,000 cells
from the mouse cortex and hippocampus, available in the
__scRNAseq__ package [@risso2025scrnaseq].

```{r here}
#| message: false
#| eval: true

library(here)
library(GraphExperiment)
library(scRNAseq)
library(scrapper)
library(bluster)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggraph)
library(patchwork)

set.seed(123) # for reproducibility
```

## Data description and processing

We will first load the data and perform standard processing steps, including
quality control, normalization, selection of highly variable genes (HVGs),
and principal component analysis (PCA), using __scrapper__
[@lun2023powering], which provides fast implementations of
common single-cell analysis steps.

```{r}
# Load data
sce <- ZeiselBrainData()
sce

# Cell types (as annotated by the authors)
table(sce$level1class)

# Quality control: remove low-quality cells based on library sizes,
# number of detected genes, and proportion of mitochondrial reads
is_mito <- rowData(sce)$featureType == "mito"
sce <- quickRnaQc.se(sce, subsets = list(mito = is_mito), filter.cells = TRUE)

# Normalization (library size factors) and log-transformation
sce <- normalizeRnaCounts.se(sce, size.factors = sce$sum)

# Feature selection and PCA
sce <- chooseRnaHvgs.se(sce, top = 2000)
sce <- runPca.se(sce, features = rowData(sce)$hvg, number = 25)

# Run t-SNE for visualization
sce <- runTsne.se(sce)
sce
```

## Building cell-cell graphs

Now, we will build a shared nearest neighbor (SNN) graph from the top
principal components with `scrapper::buildSnnGraph()`, in which
two cells are connected if they share any of their k nearest neighbors,
with edge weights defined by the rank of the shared neighbors
[@xu2015identification]. This function returns a list with
the number of vertices, the edges, and their weights, which we will
convert to an `igraph` object with cell IDs as node names. For comparison,
we will also build a kNN graph with `bluster::makeKNNGraph()`.

Note that functions that perform graph-based clustering
(e.g., `scrapper::clusterGraph.se()`) typically discard the graph or
store it in the `metadata` slot, where it is not subset along with the
cells. Using __GraphExperiment__, graphs are stored in a dedicated slot
and kept in sync with the cells.

```{r}
# Build SNN graph and convert it to an `igraph` object
pcs <- reducedDim(sce, "PCA")
snn_list <- buildSnnGraph(t(pcs), num.neighbors = 10, weight.scheme = "ranked")
snn <- make_undirected_graph(snn_list$edges, n = snn_list$vertices)
E(snn)$weight <- snn_list$weights
V(snn)$name <- colnames(sce)

# Build kNN graph
knn <- makeKNNGraph(pcs, k = 10)
V(knn)$name <- colnames(sce)

snn
```

Next, we will create a `GraphExperiment` object by coercing the
`SingleCellExperiment` object and adding both graphs to the `colGraphs` slot.

```{r}
# Create `GraphExperiment` object
ge <- as(sce, "GraphExperiment")
colGraphs(ge) <- list(snn = snn, knn = knn)

ge
```

## Graph-based clustering

We will now detect communities in each graph with the Louvain algorithm.
Community assignments will be added as node attributes, so that they are
automatically available in `colData`. We will also add node strength
(sum of edge weights) as a node attribute, since it is a measure
of how well connected a cell is to other cells.

```{r}
# Detect communities in each graph and add as node attributes
colGraphs(ge) <- lapply(colGraphs(ge), function(graph) {
    V(graph)$cluster <- as.character(membership(cluster_louvain(graph)))
    V(graph)$strength <- strength(graph)
    graph
})

# Community assignments and node strengths are now in `colData`
colData(ge)[, grepl("__", names(colData(ge)))]
```

Let's compare clusters from both graphs with each other and with cell
type annotations provided by the authors, using the adjusted Rand index (ARI).

```{r}
# Compare clusterings with ARI
c(
    SNN_vs_kNN = pairwiseRand(ge$snn__cluster, ge$knn__cluster, mode = "index"),
    SNN_vs_annotation = pairwiseRand(ge$snn__cluster, ge$level1class, mode = "index"),
    kNN_vs_annotation = pairwiseRand(ge$knn__cluster, ge$level1class, mode = "index")
)

# Cross-tabulation of SNN clusters and annotated cell types
table(ge$snn__cluster, ge$level1class)
```

Finally, let's visualize the SNN graph using the t-SNE coordinates
(stored in `reducedDims`) as layout, with cells colored by
SNN clusters (a node attribute of the graph) and by annotated cell types
(a variable in `colData`). Since all data are in the same object, and
`colGraph()` adds variables in `colData` as node attributes,
plotting is straightforward.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-dpi: 300

# Extract SNN graph with `colData` variables as node attributes
g <- colGraph(ge, "snn")
tsne <- reducedDim(ge, "TSNE")[V(g)$name, ]

# For visualization, keep only the strongest edges
g_plot <- delete_edges(g, which(E(g)$weight < quantile(E(g)$weight, 0.9)))

p1 <- ggraph(g_plot, layout = "manual", x = tsne[, 1], y = tsne[, 2]) +
    geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.05, color = "grey50") +
    geom_node_point(aes(color = factor(as.numeric(cluster))), size = 0.5) +
    guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3))) +
    theme_graph(base_family = "sans") +
    labs(color = "SNN cluster", title = "SNN graph - Louvain clusters")

p2 <- ggraph(g_plot, layout = "manual", x = tsne[, 1], y = tsne[, 2]) +
    geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.05, color = "grey50") +
    geom_node_point(aes(color = level1class), size = 0.5) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
    guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3))) +
    theme_graph(base_family = "sans") +
    labs(color = "Cell type", title = "SNN graph - annotated cell types")

wrap_plots(p1, p2, nrow = 1) +
    plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13))
```

## Subsetting

A key advantage of storing graphs in a `GraphExperiment` object is that
subsetting operations are propagated to graphs. For instance, a common
step in scRNA-seq data analysis is to subset a particular cell population
and re-cluster it to identify subpopulations. Here, we will subset
interneurons. The graphs in `colGraphs` are subset accordingly
(i.e., induced subgraphs), and cluster assignments
from the full graph are kept, so we can compare them
with clusters from the subgraph.

```{r}
# Subset interneurons
ge_int <- ge[, ge$level1class == "interneurons"]
ge_int

# Graphs were subset as well
sapply(colGraphs(ge_int), vcount)

# Re-cluster interneurons using the induced subgraph
g_int <- colGraph(ge_int, "snn")
V(g_int)$subcluster <- as.character(membership(cluster_louvain(g_int)))
colGraph(ge_int, "snn") <- g_int

# Subclusters vs annotated subtypes
table(ge_int$snn__subcluster, ge_int$level2class)
```

In summary, __GraphExperiment__ makes cell-cell graphs first-class citizens
of single-cell data analysis, allowing users to keep the graphs used for
clustering (or for other tasks, such as trajectory inference or
label propagation), along with the expression data and
dimensionality reduction results, in a single object.
